metric_rationale: The metric contrasts agreement with the validity-ordered (TTB) winner between tally-tie trials and all trials on which the equal-weight tally favors the opposite option. TTB predicts the same TTB-winner probability in both sets, so its expected value is zero for every beta and epsilon; this within-subject contrast also cancels stable response accuracy and lapse tendencies. Tallying predicts 0.5 TTB agreement on tally ties but below 0.5 on every conflict trial, yielding a distinctly positive value. Pooling the five conflict-margin conditions supplies 80 conflict observations per subject while retaining 16 tie observations, reducing binomial between-subject noise. Side-swapped pairs ensure that the contrast cannot be generated by a preference for A or B.

This is a thresholded validity-order alignment metric. Each response receives +1 when it agrees with the option favored by the highest-validity discriminating cue and -1 otherwise. Because the design balances whether A or B is that winner, the contrast is not response-side bias. Tallying has no preference on any trial and therefore predicts alignment near zero; with 96 trials, exceeding 0.25 (more than 62.5% agreement) is rare. Take The Best predicts positive alignment on every pair and should usually exceed this threshold despite lapse and softmax noise. Thresholding suppresses ordinary binomial fluctuations under Tallying and saturation among clearly TTB-like subjects, yielding low between-subject variance and a sharp theory contrast.

This is the mean signed preference for the less-marked option on the |count difference| >= 5 trials. It equals +1 when the subject chooses the option with fewer 1s and -1 when they choose the option with more 1s. Count-Gated Markedness Minimization predicts a strongly positive value because these large margins nearly saturate its count-based choice signal, whereas Tallying predicts a strongly negative value because it favors the opposite option. Restricting the contrast to margins 5 and 7 avoids weak-signal trials and should reduce parameter-driven and sampling variability. Both A/B orientations are represented equally, so stable response-side bias cannot generate the effect. The metric remains response-dependent and works unchanged for pooled data and individual-subject slices.

This is a side-balanced, weighted count-majority alignment score. It is +1 when choices consistently favor the option winning on more binary features and -1 when they consistently favor the option carrying fewer marked features. Tallying predicts a positive value on every non-tied count comparison, whereas Count-Gated Markedness Minimization predicts a negative value because its count gate favors the lower-count option. Weighting by the absolute count margin emphasizes the margin-two conditions, where both models' choice probabilities are furthest from chance in opposite directions, while retaining margin-one observations to reduce trial noise. Count-tie trials are excluded because tallying necessarily predicts chance there and their inclusion would add substantial within-subject noise. Exchanging A and B across matched trials makes the statistic insensitive to a general response-side preference, and averaging 64 informative trials per subject should yield a stable subject-level estimate.

This metric measures validity sensitivity after choices are aligned to the option with fewer marks. The predictor takes the six values +0.50, +0.08, -0.34, -0.76, -1.18, and -1.60 regardless of whether A or B is the more-marked option. Count-Gated Markedness Minimization assigns the same choice probability to every level because the count difference is always one, so it predicts a slope near zero. Smooth Integration predicts that choosing the fewer-mark option becomes progressively more likely as the validity-weighted evidence carried by the more-marked option increases, producing a positive slope. Using all 96 binary responses in one linear contrast is more stable than an endpoint-only difference, while side-alignment removes arbitrary A/B response preference.

This metric is the slope of choosing the option unmarked by the 0.99-validity expert against the full validity-weighted markedness difference. Complementary A/B presentations are recoded to the same orientation, removing response-side effects. Count-Gated Markedness Minimization predicts a condition-invariant choice probability because every trial is a count tie and the same highest-validity cue controls its tiebreak; consequently, its expected slope is zero even when schema strength differs across subjects. Smooth Integration predicts a positive graded slope because its choice probability varies continuously with the weighted difference across all six conditions. The centered within-subject slope also cancels stable subject-level response tendencies, while all 96 trials contribute to estimation, improving precision relative to an endpoint-only contrast.

This is the margin-one minus exact-tie change in choosing the option whose marked ratings are concentrated among the more valid experts. Residual-validity alignment folds the A/B-reversed trials together, so all 96 observations contribute coherently and each subject supplies 48 observations per margin condition. Crucially, adding the validity-0.75 mark changes the count margin but, because 0.75 is exactly the mean validity, leaves centered validity evidence unchanged. Smooth Integration therefore predicts that this added count/uncentered-weight signal increases choice of the high-validity-marked side, yielding a positive contrast. The discrepancy-evoked audit instead amplifies the unchanged adverse residual at margin one and predicts a negative contrast. Averaging across all eight matched configurations, their reversals, and three repetitions should keep trial noise and between-subject variance relatively low.

This is a cumulative, A/B-reversal-invariant contrast between choosing the fewer-marked product at margins five versus one. Each matched configuration contributes positively when fewer-mark choices are more prevalent at margin five and negatively when they are more prevalent at margin one. Smooth integration predicts a positive contrast because increasing the count margin adds markedness evidence while residual-validity evidence is held fixed. Residual auditing predicts a negative contrast because the strong margin-one audit decays sharply by margin five. Coding choices as ±1 and using the balanced within-subject contrast cancels stable response-side bias and much of the subject-level semantic-polarity/lapse baseline. Summing rather than averaging preserves the cumulative evidence supplied by all repetitions and remains well-defined on both pooled and single-subject data.

This is a Stouffer-style cumulative directional-evidence statistic rather than a raw fitted slope. Each subject contributes a null-standardized trial-level score contrasting fewer-mark choices on sparse versus dense discriminating displays. Trial weights follow the advocated theory's fixed discrimination-fraction saturation coordinate, are centered within subject to eliminate overall polarity and response propensity, and use all 96 observations. The competing theory predicts condition-invariant choice probabilities, so its expected centered score is zero even when subjects differ greatly in overall confidence. The advocated theory predicts systematically positive evidence because its count signal is stronger on sparse displays. Combining independent subject scores by their sum divided by the square root of subject count accumulates a weak but consistently directed within-subject signature, while application to a single-subject slice remains well-defined and yields the corresponding standardized score.

This metric is the side-balanced probability of choosing the less-marked product on margins 5, 7, 9, and 13. Unlike the failed difference score, it does not subtract the noisy margin-1 estimate, which was based on only 16 trials per subject and substantially inflated between-subject variance. It instead pools 64 large-margin trials. Under smooth integration, evidence at these margins is generally strong enough that choice approaches each subject's semantic-polarity/lapse ceiling. Under the competing theory, the count representation has already saturated, but its bounded asymptotic evidence still produces appreciably less decisive choices. Thus the theories differ in the absolute large-margin choice level, while side reversal removes response-position bias and pooling yields a relatively stable subject-level estimate.

This is the proportion of choices favoring the option whose marks come from the lower-validity experts, restricted to the three strongest validity conflicts (m=7, 11, and 18). It pools 48 repeated trials per subject and folds the A/B reversals into the same orientation, providing substantially lower sampling variance than a single-condition contrast. Smooth Integration predicts a large preference for this option because its unattenuated validity evidence is already strong at these levels. The advocated load-capacity theory predicts choices much closer to 0.5 because 37-feature display load sharply attenuates the same validity residual. Excluding the weak m=1, 2, and 4 conditions increases the expected theory gap while retaining enough trials for a stable subject-level estimate.

The metric is the within-subject linear slope of orientation-corrected, adverse-aligned choices across absolute count margins 1 through 5. Smooth Integration predicts a sizable positive slope because its evidence continues increasing at every added mean-validity mark. Dual-Timescale Integration predicts a slope near zero because its count accumulator has already nearly saturated at margin 1 while the centered-validity residual remains fixed. Using all five margins and both A/B orientations yields a lower-variance estimate than an endpoint difference, and the balanced repetitions make the pooled estimate directly comparable to the per-subject estimates.

This is a reliability-aligned, matched diagnostic-load contrast. Choices are first recoded so that 1 always denotes selection of the option favored by the signed centered-validity residual, making the A/B-reversed trials reinforce rather than cancel one another. The zero-sum coefficients approximate the nonlinear attenuation profile predicted by Resource-Adaptive Diagnostic Field Integration: a large contribution from the organized four-cue condition, modest contributions from intermediate conditions, and increasingly negative weights once diffuse evidence and overload dominate. Semantic-Polarity Smooth Integration predicts the same aligned choice probability at every load because its count and weighted-validity evidence are held constant, so its expected contrast is approximately zero for every parameter setting. Centering the weights removes overall polarity, lapse, and reliability-sensitivity levels, while using all 96 trials keeps per-subject sampling variance lower than a simple endpoint difference. Positive values indicate the advocated signature of stronger reliability-aligned choice at low diagnostic load than in dense displays.

This is the within-subject decline in choosing the option with fewer marked ratings from sparse diagnostic fields (7–19 discriminating cues) to overloaded fields (27–35 cues). Coding choices relative to the sign of the count difference combines the A/B-reversed trials and removes arbitrary response-side orientation. Semantic-Polarity Smooth Integration receives exactly the same count and weighted evidence at every density, so it predicts a contrast near zero. Resource-Adaptive Diagnostic Field Integration selectively compresses its fixed, large count margin after diagnostic demand exceeds its span, predicting a sizable positive sparse-minus-dense contrast. Pooling four sparse levels and three dense levels uses 84 trials per subject, reducing binomial variance while excluding the ambiguous transition condition at 23 cues.
